issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For an adult male sexual assault survivor, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the selected items and formulation. The other triggers (related news, motorcycle noise) plausibly cue intrusive memory reactivation, and the memory items are all intrusion/emotion based. 'Being around children' implies a distinct trauma meaning or developmental context that is not reflected anywhere in Memory, Threat, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies. Given the formulation is dominated by Triggers ↔ Memory links, this trigger stands out as insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory content and is the one item most likely to be incoherent.

vignette:
For forty-eight-year-old Mako, the assault happened on a Friday night, after a roofing job in a coastal town where the crew had stopped for drinks. He had been the designated driver, nursing a single soda while the others laughed and drank, and when he left early to get some air near the truck, a colleague followed him out. The colleague's breath smelled of whiskey. Mako had known him for years. That was what made the next few minutes-the hand clamped over his mouth, the pressure against the gravel, the voice hissing that nobody would believe a man who said he was attacked by a man-so impossible to reconcile afterward. He never told anyone at work. He told his wife, Leilani, a few days later, but only the barest facts, and then he asked her not to bring it up again.

In the months that followed, Mako found that his life had become a series of small, constant calculations. The first thing he noticed was the motorcycle. A neighbor's son had a dirt bike that he rode up and down the block on Saturday afternoons. The sound-that low, throaty rumble-would hit Mako in the chest before he could even name it as a sound. His hands would go cold. His shoulders would lock. He began timing his weekends around it, leaving the house before the boy typically started riding, or retreating to the basement with noise-canceling headphones. Leilani asked why he was spending so much time downstairs. He said he was organizing tools.

Then there was the alcohol smell. He had never been a heavy drinker, but now the scent of beer or liquor, even from a car window in traffic, would make his stomach drop. He started avoiding the aisle at the grocery store. He stopped going to barbecues where people might have coolers. When Leilani poured herself a glass of wine after dinner, he would quietly leave the room, claiming he needed to check the gutters or start the laundry. She had begun to look at him differently, he could tell. Her questions were gentle, but they were questions.

The news was its own kind of trap. He had never paid much attention to headlines before, but now every story about an assault-any assault, anywhere-seemed to be aimed directly at him. He would be scrolling his phone and feel his vision narrow, the words on the screen becoming too immediate, too physical. He deleted the news apps. He told himself it was just a way to simplify his life. But what he was really doing was trying to seal himself off from anything that might crack the fragile surface he had constructed.

That surface was built on two things: keeping busy and controlling what he ate. Mako worked as a roofer, and the job had always been physically demanding, but now he pushed himself harder than necessary. He volunteered for the heaviest loads, the steepest pitches, the longest days. When he came home exhausted, he would eat a small, precise meal-exactly the same portion, exactly the same foods, night after night. It was the only thing he could control. His body had been a place where something terrible happened. If he could regulate every calorie, every ounce of exertion, maybe he could keep that body from betraying him again.

But the memories did not respect his systems. Sometimes he would be driving to a job site, his mind blank, and then suddenly he would feel it: the full, crushing weight of that night, the gravel digging into his back, the smell of whiskey and sweat, the shame. There was no image with it, no clear picture, just the emotion-raw and complete, as if the event were happening in that moment rather than a year ago. Other times, the memory came with unbearable vividness, more real than anything happening around him. He could see the pattern of the gravel, the angle of the streetlight, the exact shade of the sky. And then there was the grief. When he remembered the person he had been before that night-the easy laugh, the trust in other men, the sense that his body was his own-he would feel a sorrow so deep that it hollowed him out. He had lost something he could not name, and he could not stop mourning it.

What finally brought him to a clinic was a moment on a roof. He had been standing at the edge, securing a shingle, when a motorcycle passed on the street below. The sound hit him, and for a second-just a second-his body went rigid, and he looked down at the drop and thought, It would be so easy. He did not want to die. But the thought terrified him more than the assault had. He told Leilani that night. The next morning, she made the appointment.

Now, sitting in an intake office, Mako keeps his hands flat on his knees. He is afraid of what it will mean to talk about it in detail. He is afraid that if he lets himself feel the grief fully, he will not be able to stop. But he is also, somewhere beneath the fear, hoping that someone can help him find a way back to the person he used to be-or at least to a version of himself that does not have to spend every waking moment running from a ghost.
